title: PASTA Threat Modelling
summary: PASTA, the Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis, is a seven stage, risk centric threat modelling method that starts from business objectives rather than from a list of technical flaws. It was published by Tony UcedaVelez and Marco Morana and is described in the book Risk Centric Threat Modeling. The stages move from defining business objectives, to defining the technical scope, to decomposing the application, to analysing threats, to enumerating weaknesses, to simulating attacks against those weaknesses, and finally to analysing risk and impact. What it constrains is the order of reasoning: you cannot discuss a weakness until you have tied it to an attacker goal and a business asset. That makes it heavier than lightweight methods such as STRIDE, so teams tend to reserve PASTA for high value systems where an attacker's motivation and the resulting business loss both need to be documented. The common mistake is treating it as a checklist that ends with a diagram: the simulation and risk analysis stages are the ones that produce the prioritisation, and skipping them leaves an abstract model with no decision attached.

exercises.title: PASTA Threat Modelling - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: PASTA Threat Modelling - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: PASTA Threat Modelling - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: PASTA Threat Modelling - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.

beginner.definition: PASTA is a way to study a system before attackers do. It is a step by step method that links business goals to the technical parts of a system. Then it looks at how an attacker could reach those goals. The result is a list of risks with reasons.
beginner.whyItMatters: Teams often fix the technical bugs that look worst on a scanner report. Those bugs may not matter to the business at all. PASTA forces you to start from what the business needs to protect. Then you spend your limited time on the attacks that would really hurt. It also gives you written reasons you can show to managers.
howItWorks: Write down the business goals of the system and what would happen if each one failed.
Describe the technical scope, including the parts you will study and the parts you will not.
Break the system into smaller parts, such as logins, databases and data flows between them.
List the attackers who care about this system and the goals they would want to reach.
Find the weaknesses that could help an attacker move toward those goals.
Walk through realistic attack paths and score the risk each one carries for the business.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital night desk. The goal is that the right patient gets the right medicine at the right time. A narrow guard might only check the front door lock. A PASTA style review starts with the medicine goal. Then it asks who would want to disrupt it. It follows the path from the front door to the drug cabinet to the computer that holds prescriptions. Each step is a place where something can go wrong. At the end, the desk manager knows the three fixes that reduce the most risk. The long list of small things can wait.
takeaways: Start from business goals, not from a scanner report.
Tie every weakness to an attacker goal and a real asset.
The final risk stage is what turns a model into decisions.

objectives: Explain what PASTA is and why it is described as risk centric rather than technology centric.
List the stages of PASTA and describe the question each stage answers.
Describe how PASTA differs from a lightweight method such as STRIDE, and when each is appropriate.
Apply the business objective stage to a small system and identify the assets worth protecting.
Show how a weakness is linked to an attacker goal before it is prioritised.
Explain why skipping the simulation and risk analysis stages weakens the whole exercise.
